title: Male circumcision | NHS inform
text:
Male circumcision
Male circumcision is a type of surgery where the foreskin (skin that covers the head of the penis) is removed.
It may be available on the NHS for medical reasons or non-medical reasons.
Medical reasons for circumcision
Tight foreskin (phimosis)
The most common reason for a circumcision is when the foreskin is tight. This might mean the foreskin itself doesn’t pull back easily or causes discomfort when it does. This is known as phimosis.
Alternative treatments may be an option, such as topical steroid creams. Your GP will discuss and agree the best treatment option for you.
Paraphimosis
Phimosis can sometimes lead to paraphimosis, which is when the foreskin won’t go back to it’s original position after being pulled back. This causes the head of the penis to swell and become painful. In these cases, immediate treatment is needed in hospital.
Balanitis
Balanitis is a recurring infection that causes the foreskin and head of the penis to become inflamed.
Depending on what is causing the balanitis, a GP might prescribe:
mild steroid cream or ointment
antifungal cream or ointments
antibiotics
Circumcision may be considered if the infection continues to come back.
Penile cancer
Penile cancer
is a rare type of cancer that occurs on the skin of the penis or within the penis. In some cases, circumcision may be used to treat the affected area.
Non-medical reasons for circumcision
Circumcision may also be carried out for non-medical reasons.
Religious beliefs
Circumcision is common in certain religions, for example in Jewish and Muslim communities.
Some parents’ religion or beliefs mean they will want their male child to be circumcised as soon as possible after birth.
Circumcision for religious reasons can be carried out by the NHS in Scotland as long as doctors are satisfied that the operation is in the child’s best interests.
If this is something you as a parent are considering, you should discuss this with your midwife before your child is born. Then you can request referral from your GP at your child’s 6 week check-up.
NHS Scotland guidelines state that circumcision for religious reasons should:
be carried out in hospital by trained paediatric surgeons under general anaesthesia
take place when the male child is between 6 and 9 months old
Before any surgical procedure, it’s important to understand the benefits, risks and possible side effects.
What happens during a circumcision
Circumcisions are usually carried out on an outpatient or day-case basis. This means you don’t have to stay in hospital overnight. You might be asked not to eat beforehand.
Before the procedure, you’ll talk to the surgical team who will discuss what will happen. You can ask any questions you might have.
You’ll either be given:
general anaesthetic
– you’ll be unconscious during the procedure, or
local anaesthetic
– you’ll be conscious but your penis and the areas around it will be numb
Less commonly, you might have a spinal anaesthetic. This means you won’t be able to feel anything below your waist.
During the circumcision, the foreskin is removed from the head of the penis using a scalpel or surgical scissors. Dissolvable stitches will be used to stitch the skin together.
Recovery
When you’re able to leave the hospital, you’ll be given advice on how to recover at home.
Speak to your GP practice if:
You’ve had a circumcision recently and have:
any concerns
difficulty peeing
a high temperature (fever)
increased redness
bleeding
continual pain
Some of this can be a sign of infection, which can be treated by your GP.
You’ll be told what things you can do and what things you should try to avoid while recovering. For example:
when you’re able to drive
when you’re able to go back to work – you might need about a week off to rest and recover
when you’re able to have sex – this is usually around 4 weeks after the procedure
It takes around 10 days for your penis to heal after having a circumcision.
You might experience some pain and discomfort for a few days after the procedure. You can take painkillers to help with this.
